title: Teddy Young: Royal Navy sailor in court accused of preparing to spy for Russia
description: A junior Royal Navy sailor accused of preparing to spy for Russia has appeared in court.Able Seaman Teddy Young, who specialised in warfare intelligen
body: A junior Royal Navy sailor accused of preparing to spy for Russia has appeared in court.Able Seaman Teddy Young, who specialised in warfare intelligence, allegedly retained UK defence and intelligence material that he had access to and made preparations to disclose sensitive information, a court was told.The 24-year-old appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday after being charged under the National Security Act.The BBC understands that the allegations against Young include translating a message into Russian and looking for a web portal that invited people to submit information to Russia.Wearing a police-issue grey sweatshirt, Young spoke in court to confirm his name, date of birth and his address in Clapham, near Bedford.He is formally charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for disclosing protected information, and obtaining, copying, recording or retaining protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.The charges cover a period between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025."The allegation is that while serving as a Royal Navy warfare intelligence rating with high level security clearance and intelligence-system access, Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young accessed and retained sensitive UK defence and intelligence material and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power," the Crown Prosecution Service told the court in a written summary of the allegations.Police said the alleged offences were not related to the recent RAF Fairford incident that resulted in a number of arrests after suspicious activity was reported near the base. In total, seven men have been arrested and later released on bail in connection with the incident, which is being investigated by counter-terror police.Young was arrested at his home address in Bedfordshire on Tuesday.He is the first member of the armed forces to be charged under the new National Security Act 2023.Cdr Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. "We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."A Royal Navy spokesperson confirmed a service member had been charged and added: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage."Judge Annabel Pilling remanded Young in custody. He will next appear at the Old Bailey on 16 October.

schema.headline: Teddy Young: Royal Navy sailor in court accused of preparing to spy for Russia

title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
description: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the
body: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

schema.headline: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design

title: Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says
description: Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, t
body: Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence. Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.The next stage in this legal dispute will be a behind-closed-doors hearing over whether the police can still retain material seized from Mountbatten-Windsor's homes under alternative powers designed for situations like this.The error that has led to Thames Valley Police accepting the search warrants were unlawful relates to the particular power the judge permitted the force to use when its officers raided the properties.Strict legal safeguards on searches bar the police from automatically seizing sensitive material without thinking through in advance the need to take it.Examples of that material include advice from a suspect's lawyer or material which does not really belong to them, such as copies of confidential work-related papers from an employer.In practice, if the police find such material during a search, they should return it rather than use it in their investigation.The category of search warrant that was granted by the court in this instance did not take into account the possibility of such protected material being seized.However, the law says police can in fact seize that kind of material - or potentially retain it in the event of an error - providing they pass some extra tests.Thames Valley Police must now convince a judge that the material is likely to be of "substantial value" to their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor and, ultimately, potential evidence to present to a court. So while the force has conceded the search warrant was unlawful, a judge will have to decide whether this alternative search power, with its extra safeguards, justifies them keeping and using the material after all.

schema.headline: Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says

title: Gaten Matarazzo swaps Stranger Things for Rent in West End
description: Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big d
body: Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big difference.You don't get the luxury of "thirty takes" to get it right in front of a live audience.The former Stranger Things star's currently playing Mark in a modern revival of rock musical Rent on London's West End.He tells BBC Newsbeat that having a proper schedule and remembering to stay hydrated makes a "refreshing change" from filming the Netflix smash-hit that made him famous.Matarazzo shot to fame in 2016 as endearing super-geek Dustin Henderson - a role he calls "the greatest honour of his life".The saga finally concluded last December after five seasons, and there's been interest in what the show's cast will do next."It's something you do inevitably step away from," says Matarazzo "We finished filming in 2024 - there's no more show to film.""I still love what I do very much, I want to keep on doing it."Casting big names from TV and film in theatre shows is a growing trend, and one that sometimes provokes accusations of cashing in. But Matarazzo has plenty of stage experience, having performed on Broadway when he was a child.He says the time commitment involved meant it was impossible to "blend both worlds"."My favourite part of theatre specifically is the schedule," he says."Going to bed at the same time and waking up at the same time."I've always thrived under a schedule and when I don't have one I feel insane."In Rent, Matarazzo plays struggling film-maker Mark, who chronicles and narrates the lives of his friends.It has been 30 years since the show first opened off-Broadway in New York, but the actor says there are "certain songs that weirdly resonate now"."What You Own, which feels like a reflection on information overload, is incredibly relevant," he says."That's really fun to sing in context of today."When it was first performed, Rent shone a light on young friends and artists living in late 1980s and early 1990s New York during the HIV/Aids crisis.It was considered groundbreaking at the time for tackling social taboos and centering stories of LGBT people. Writer Jonathan Larson died suddenly the night before its premiere. Matarazzo's co-star, Travis Ross, who plays Roger, says the show's themes still "ring true" today.The 25-year-old says having Rent tends to attract people who "care so deeply" about the show's message, resulting in a connection between actors and the audience.He calls it a "really beautiful community-driven piece of art". Both Ross and Matarazzo are keen to acknowledge their fellow cast members and point out Rent is "an ensemble" piece."In the same way we get our moments to tell the story there's also ten other people who get their moments to tell the story as well," says Ross.Many of those in the audience will be there to watch Matarazzo, and he says he's determined to get the role right."I'm on stage for the majority of the show and singing the whole time," he says."It's not anything that's particularly high or out of my range, it's actually a part that I think fits nicely in my pocket."But it's just so much singing, and making sure I'm doing it correctly is essential," he says.Matarazzo also plans to embrace his return to the stage."Once we're in the run it will be great," he says. "I just always love the opportunity to start and finish a character arc and story in real time."You don't get an opportunity to do that when you're filming." Speaking of which - if he ever got the call to go back to Hawkins and step into Dustin's shoes, would he take the chance?"If that happens, that's great, and if not, that's completely fine."I've loved doing the show so much, it's literally the greatest honour of my life."Rent is at The Tom Stoppard Theatre, London.  Gaten Matarazzo is booked to perform until 10 January.

schema.headline: Gaten Matarazzo swaps Stranger Things for Rent in West End

title: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
description: At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue official
body: At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across Ukraine and a heavy increase in civilian casualties. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who together with Zelensky visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky, said the attack showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched by Putin in 2022 - a claim rejected by Ukraine and its allies as baseless.Donbas is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall.  In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.Kramatorsk city council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population"."Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said. Russia has in recent weeks been launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing virtually non-stop.On Thursday, Kyiv police said four people were killed and two injured in the latest Russian attack on the city.The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into underground shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport. Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's key infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.Kyiv's metro network - which millions of residents rely on - on Thursday briefly halted all its train traffic due to a voltage drop from "external power centres". Trains later started moving again - but at greater intervals, local officials said.Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine". Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little  chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics. Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.On Thursday, Russian state-run media reported that a number of websites in the country were inaccessible following a Ukrainian drone attack on a data centre of Yandex - Russia's largest search engine.

schema.headline: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge

title: Venezuela's ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
description: Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture. Th
body: Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture. The fresh charges against the couple were made public on Thursday and are in addition to the drug-trafficking and weapons charges already brought against them, which they have denied. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been in custody since January in a detention centre in Brooklyn, where they were taken after US forces seized them in a pre-dawn raid on their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas. Barry J Pollack, Maduro's attorney, said his client denies the new charges and looks forward to his day in court.Federal prosecutors also announced on Thursday that Flores was added to the earlier narco-terrorism charge.The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027. Both are being held in a detention centre in Brooklyn and are expected to remain there after Flores's request to be moved to house arrest was denied by a judge on Thursday.The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens who were being held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power.The superseding indictment unsealed on Thursday accuses the former presidential couple of "entrenching themselves in power" by presiding "over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens". According to the indictment, the torture included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture".The prosecutors allege that the psychological torture included threats to kill victims' families, including children. "All of this was done to ensure that  Maduro and Flores retained their power," prosecutors said outside the courthouse on Thursday. "This conduct, we allege, has caused significant harm to Americans, to US citizens", prosecutors said, calling it "the epitome of corruption".The prosecution accuses Flores of having played a key role in the development of the repressive system, ordering that individuals be tortured and even receiving updates on the torture of specific prisoners.The court document alleges that she did so in order to protect members of her family who were involved in illegal activities. The allegations contained in the superseding indictment echo many of the accusations long made by prisoners who have been released from detention in Venezuela.Javier Tarazona, the head of a human rights group in Venezuela, told BBC Mundo's Norberto Paredes earlier this year how he and his brother were held in a tiny punishment cell for 46 days after being arbitrarily arrested. Another former inmate, Ángel Godoy, told BBC Mundo that he was kept isolated for  months and not allowed to contact his wife, who was in turn kept in the dark about his whereabouts. The allegations listed in the superseding indictment made public on Thursday relate to cases during Maduro's time in power.After his ouster, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim leader with the backing of the Trump administration.While hundreds of political prisoners have been released under an amnesty law since she has taken over power, more than 300 still remain behind bars, according to prisoners' rights group Foro Penal.The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has warned that his office has received reports alleging that detainees continue to be tortured even after the seizure of Maduro. Türk said in March that "structural and systemic human rights concerns" had persisted in Venezuela despite Maduro's ousting.Venezuela's foreign minister at the time accused Türk of parroting the agenda of "extremists" by citing the allegations.

schema.headline: Venezuela's ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture

title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
description: Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others
body: Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause."It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees."There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own."They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government. On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday.Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years. When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent."When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista. In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern. A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market. Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation. He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain."When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes. The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs. Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand. Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period. That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building."It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries. A study by El País found that, in real terms, the average Spaniard had 5% less spending power than a decade ago, due to taxes, social security and inflation. The average monthly salary in the Madrid region is €1,550 (£1,314; $1,738)."No worker should have to spend 75% or 80% of their salary on rent, because what are they supposed to eat?" says Francisco Pardo, an 81-year-old retired taxi driver, who sympathises with the protesters, during a visit to the tent city in Madrid. "Many workers don't even earn €2,000 [per month]."The case of Maricarmen has suddenly made the housing crisis an urgent topic of discussion, not just in Madrid's Puerta del Sol but across the country. The question now is whether a consensus can be reached on how to solve it.

schema.headline: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis

title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
description: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.It issued the upda
body: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals.One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her.The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know. "What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said.With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls.The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed."Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said. "We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached. Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action. But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity."Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio."Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information". "We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

schema.headline: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds

title: Schoolgirl told teacher 'Sir, I've been stabbed', court hears
description: A schoolgirl who was stabbed by a masked fellow pupil at school described how she told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed" after the attack.Police were
body: A schoolgirl who was stabbed by a masked fellow pupil at school described how she told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed" after the attack.Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March, following reports that a 15-year-old girl had been stabbed in the back.The defendant, who is now 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, has denied a charge of attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.In a police interview played to the jury at King's Lynn Crown Court, the girl said she had been in "panic mode" and felt numb and weak.Describing the attack, which took place in a corridor, she said she had seen a masked person dressed "head to toe in black, no school uniform whatsoever".The boy did not say anything to her and she did not recognise him, she added. She said she turned away and it "felt like he touched me on the shoulder, then it felt like he punched me".She said she "didn't know I was stabbed at this point" but after turning into a classroom, "I went 'Sir, I've been stabbed.'"The girl said the school lockdown bell sounded and staff gave first aid.Of the incident itself, she said that once she had opened the door, "I felt sharp pain shooting through my back, I went like that and it was blood all over my hands".She said in the interview, carried out days after the incident: "I don't think it's hit me properly yet."It's just a bit of a shock."

schema.headline: Schoolgirl told teacher 'Sir, I've been stabbed', court hears

title: South Africa vs Australia: Pat Cummins speaks to Usman Khawaja about autobiography
description: Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about p
body: Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations.On Friday, Australia will begin their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering scandal erupted in Cape Town in 2018.At the time, captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft were banned for their part in the plot.Since then, the four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including Cummins, have denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan to cheat.The quartet, who released a joint statement about the episode in 2021, are once again set to be united in the first Test against South Africa in Durban.Khawaja played in all four Tests in 2018 and retired from international cricket in January. His autobiography will be released in November."Uz gave me a buzz a few weeks back that he is releasing a book," said Cummins. "He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries."Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times."It was dealt with then and all I can say is that as a group, we have moved on and we are very happy with the last eight to nine years how we have been as a group and evolved and obviously my focus is on captaining the cricket team."At the time of the ball-tampering controversy, Smith explained it was devised by the "leadership group" of the Australian team on the third day of the third Test in Cape Town. Bancroft was caught rubbing sandpaper on the ball the same day.While Smith, Warner and Bancroft – all batters – were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."Days after Bancroft's interview was published, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again."We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands."And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage."We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."Earlier this week, left-arm seamer Starc referenced the scandal when he said: "What's left to come out after eight years?"And, speaking on Thursday, Cummins said the episode was "a long time ago"."It's nothing new," the 33-year-old told ABC. "We've spoken about it a little bit. If the crowd gets rowdy or whatever, if someone needs an extra helping hand, we're around."To be honest, it's so long ago and we, as a group, move on from things pretty quickly. It hasn't taken up too much of our time."The trip to South Africa is the first in a year of high-profile away series for Australia. After what appears to be a stern challenge against New Zealand in their home summer, Cummins' men then travel to India and defend the Ashes in England next year.With all-rounder Cameron Green ruled out because of injury, the tourists are likely to choose between Cooper Connolly and Nic Maddinson for a place in the middle order.On a Durban pitch expected to turn, South Africa have included two spinners – Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer - in their XI.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Pat Cummins speaks to Usman Khawaja about autobiography

title: RAF Molesworth: Men arrested on suspicion of trespass at US base
description: Two Latvian men were arrested after a fence was breached at an RAF base used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations, counter-terroris
body: Two Latvian men were arrested after a fence was breached at an RAF base used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations, counter-terrorism police have said.The alert was raised when a Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrol at RAF Molesworth identified an abandoned vehicle at about 22:00 BST on Wednesday.Searches revealed a small breach of the fence at the site in Cambridgeshire, and a few hours later, police said the pair were arrested inside the perimeter.The two men are aged 36 and 32 and live in the UK, the Met Police said.The force's Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating and commander Helen Flanagan said officers were not currently linking it to the high-profile incident in Gloucestershire."We're very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week," said Flanagan.However, she stressed the inquiry was in its "very early stages".Seventh man bailed in connection with RAF Fairford incidentThey were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage - after Cambridgeshire Police officers joined the search - and were taken to a local station.The pair were later arrested on suspicion of an offence under Section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, external – namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.RAF Molesworth is home to the US's intelligence operations centres for Europe and Africa, as well as a Nato intelligence hub.It is not used as a flying station.

schema.headline: RAF Molesworth: Men arrested on suspicion of trespass at US base

title: 'Ominous signs' of winter pressures as NHS waiting list grows
description: There are "ominous signs" that winter pressures are already affecting the NHS in England, according to senior health leaders.The warning comes as new
body: There are "ominous signs" that winter pressures are already affecting the NHS in England, according to senior health leaders.The warning comes as new data reveals the waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row.An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.The numbers are the highest since October 2025 and have raised questions over whether the NHS will meet a government target of treating 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.The rise in waiting lists comes despite the NHS in England delivering what were described as record levels of planned, elective care over the summer, while demand for services also reached its highest level ever.A record 4.7 million planned treatments, procedures and appointments occurred across June, July and August – more than in any previous summer.But both A&Es and ambulance services also saw a record number of patients for the month of September.NHS England's national medical director, Professor Frankie Swords, warned that despite the progress delivered by frontline teams, winter pressure was already building."Staff are already seeing the ominous early signs of pressure, with more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year, and unfortunately many people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she said.The NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, says the government in England is not going to achieve its manifesto promise of hitting the 18-week hospital waiting time target by the end of the parliament in 2029.That 18-week target hasn't been hit for a decade.A separate analysis by the Health Foundation think-tank said progress on cutting waiting times had stalled over the past year, with referrals on to the waiting list rising at a much quicker rate than the number of patients being treated.Sir Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance which represents NHS trusts, said: "The NHS continues to respond to record demand for care, but the relentless growth in demand for services is putting NHS staff under real pressure."Francesca Cavallaro, of the Health Foundation, said: "Thanks to the hard work of staff, the NHS has made progress in bringing down waiting times, but a rise in referrals mean that the service is having to run faster just to stand still and the prospects of meeting the government's pledge are receding."Andy Burnham's government have yet to set out whether they will give the 18-week target the same priority as it had under Keir Starmer, but our analysis shows the pledge is becoming increasingly hard to deliver."There will be concern too that the pressures of a long, hot summer have merged almost seamlessly into the pressures associated with the winter months. More patients, including children, have been arriving at A&E departments with flu and other respiratory viruses.The number of patients seen within four hours in A&Es last month fell to 74.4%,  down from 75.0% in August.The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted – what is known as "corridor care" – stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August.That has alarmed Dr Vicky Price, president of the Society for Acute Medicine."A 13% year-on-year rise in 12-hour emergency department waits as winter approaches should set alarm bells ringing. "More than 50,000 patients waited over 12 hours from the decision to admit to admission in September - 1,686 people every day. "These are not just numbers."They represent vulnerable people who are waiting far too long for a bed and staff trying to deliver safe care in overcrowded emergency departments."The government says the 18-week mark could still be achieved, saying it was investing in NHS buildings and equipment to make services more productive.It also pointed to disruption to care that was caused by the strikes by resident doctors, a dispute which has now been settled.But the strain that services are feeling in September, before winter has even really got going, will be a cause for concern among NHS leaders and their political bosses alike.

schema.headline: 'Ominous signs' of winter pressures as NHS waiting list grows

title: Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women
description: Police Scotland has said 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.Chief constable Jo Farrell s
body: Police Scotland has said 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.Chief constable Jo Farrell said she expected more would face sanctions over their behaviour following a spate of former officers being convicted for sexual offences.Farrell said a review into the handling of the case surrounding officer Alan Greer – who was exposed as a serial rapist after taking his own life – was under way.She added about 8,000 members of staff were still to be "re-vetted" for their roles after a change in regulations earlier this year.First minister John Swinney said he had "full confidence" in Police Scotland and the renewed vetting process.In an interview with BBC Scotland News, Farrell described the scale of violence against women and girls in Scotland as an "epidemic", and that police forces were not immune to the problem.She said: "We've got in the order of between currently 40 and 50 people currently suspended, so not at work, who are being investigated for offences that relate to violence against women and girls."Those investigations are at various stages."Farrell said that between 300 and 400 officers had now been re-vetted as part of new rules brought in following the murder of Sarah Everard by Met Police officer Wayne Couzens.About 6,000 officers and 2,000 civilian staff still have to go through the new vetting process.She said the rules would make it easier to "exit people" found to be unsuitable to serve in the force."It's only now during this year there has been a change in the vetting regime. So for the first time, if an officer fails their vetting, they can be exited from policing," she said."So that is a very recent change, and a welcome change from my point of view. Up until that point there were no opportunities to exit people from the organisation."Farrell added: "My focus is on identifying where there is wrongdoing, criminality, particularly in relation to violence against women and girls and if that has been committed by our officers and our staff, that we identify it and we ensure that those people feel the full force of the law."Craig Naylor, HM Chief Inspector of Constabulary, said incidents involving officers were taken "very seriously" when reported to Police Scotland.He said: "We've done work over the last number of years on vetting and police conduct on a number of areas that have highlighted where Police Scotland can improve and they are making improvements in those areas."However, police officers are members of society and our society has violent offenders within it so they are likely to be further offenders within Scotland within policing."Naylor added: "For me, what we've seen with the recent incidents with Mr Greer, with Constable Petrie recently, have shown that when something is reported to Police Scotland they take it very seriously, they put their best resources onto it, they investigate it and they get convictions."

schema.headline: Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women

title: Singapore Grand Prix: George Russell says he will take another grid penalty this season
description: "I knew I was going to have a penalty," Russell said. "The plan was always to go in Austin, and obviously Singapore is the second hardest track to ove
body: "I knew I was going to have a penalty," Russell said. "The plan was always to go in Austin, and obviously Singapore is the second hardest track to overtake on on the calendars. So you would never choose to do it (here)."But we have no engines because of all of the various failures, so there was no engine I could have reverted to from earlier in the season. With the failure I had to take it."We don't have the (upgrade) this weekend, and because there are seven races remaining, you can either choose to roll the dice and hope it lasts for seven races, but also suffer a performance offset (as the engine degrades), or just accept I'll be taking another penalty."Antonelli will also likely have another back-of-the-grid penalty when the upgraded engine is introduced, following his previous one at the Italian Grand Prix, which he won from 19th on the grid.Russell will also be reverting to an older specification car in Singapore this weekend.Mercedes introduced an aerodynamic upgrade in Malaysia last weekend, but it did not give the car the performance uplift expected.So in an attempt to prove whether that was because of idiosyncrasies to do with the Sepang track or a problem with the upgrade itself, Mercedes is splitting the specification of their cars.Russell will drive the specification with which he won in Azerbaijan, the week before Malaysia, while Antonelli will run the new spec.Russell said: "I actually asked a question already on Friday in Sepang. At the end of the day it's the car I'm reverting to is a car that was on pole by 0.8secs and Kimi won the race before, so it's important to remember the context. It's not like reverting back to a launch car."Given the circumstances of the grid penalty as well, it just seemed like a no-brainer. For me, unfortunately we're not going to be fighting for a podium this weekend, it's exceptionally unlikely, so it's more important for us to try and understand, was Malaysia a one-off or was it the upgrade?"Russell's retirement in Malaysia, along with Antonelli finishing second to Red Bull's Max Verstappen, meant the Italian's lead in the drivers' championship has extended to 84 points.Both Mercedes drivers have suffered reliability problems this year but Russell believes his season has been disproportionately affected by factors outside his control."I've probably had more failures this year than I've had in the three seasons put together, and of course it's tough to take," he said."If I'm being 100% fair with myself, as I've said before, the performance this season hasn't been strong enough, and it probably would have affected me more if I'd have still been in the fight."But obviously the pressure and the momentum, every setback has an impact on that momentum."Since the start of the year (an engine failure) in Canada was the big one, and then, you know, the drive-through penalty in Monaco. The loss at the weekend has basically compromised two weekends for me."Two races, Silverstone and Spa, with the PU issues we had (involving a loss of performance from the engine), it's been pretty incredible how things have panned out this year, but I think just focus on what you can control."

schema.headline: Singapore Grand Prix: George Russell says he will take another grid penalty this season

title: Mum blamed for baby's death at Telford hospital calls for change in NHS
description: Poppy Russell died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford.  She was just 12 hours old.  During her pregnancy her mother told midwives
body: Poppy Russell died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford.  She was just 12 hours old.  During her pregnancy her mother told midwives that she had tokophobia, a fear of natural birth and wanted a caesarean section.  Katie said she was repeatedly told however that she "couldn't just ask for a c-section."When she went into labour, Katie was induced and then "we were left in a room for long periods of time where I had no care," she explained. "Finally, when we got into the labour suite, I wasn't monitored appropriately and they missed signs that Poppy was in distress."In a bitter irony, Poppy had to be delivered by emergency caesarean.  By then however, she had developed a hypoxic brain injury and died later the same day.  An inquest into her death found that had Poppy been born an hour earlier, she would have survived.The Shrewsbury and Telford NHS Trust (SaTH), which ran the hospital, subsequently blamed Katie for her daughter's death.  They said she had refused foetal monitoring; the inquest concluded that was untrue."The trust left us in an appalling position," said Neil Russell.  "Not only were they found to have neglected our care, but in the months and years following, we uncovered that members of staff had tried to cover it up.  “Losing your daughter is one thing, but then to find that there was a cavalcade of lies was almost as bad."Following the inquest in 2023 the trust said: "We recognise there were failings in the care we provided and we are truly sorry."It said the death of any baby was a "tragedy" and promised improvements to maternity services. In March 2024, the couple had a meeting with the trust to discuss all that had happened.  From the discussions, Neil and Katie decided they needed to honour Poppy.   "The first conversations about Poppy's Promise were about being human," said Neil, 45. "It spun from our treatment, and not being treated like human beings."Poppy's Promise is based on four care principles:Compassion - showing kindnessAcknowledgement - recognising a patient's feelingsRespect - valuing their opinionEmpowerment - involving patients in their care"It's seeing the person, not the diagnosis.  It's someone coming into a room holding your hand, someone acknowledging the fact that this is difficult for you," said Katie.Even in the midst of her poor care at the time of her daughter's death, Katie, 41, vividly remembers one midwife who showed some compassion.  "She came in and said, 'how are you doing? I just want to hug you.' "She sat with me and she cried with me and she said, 'this should never have happened,' and that will always stay with me because it's exactly what I needed at that point."At the time of Poppy's death, SaTH was in the middle of a large maternity inquiry.  The review found that 201 babies and nine mothers might have survived with better care.As part of its improvement programme, the trust is now rolling out Poppy's Promise to all 8,000 staff. As well as reminding its existing employees of the principles of compassionate care, the trust has embedded a question about it into its recruitment processes.The most important part of the training is "to remind me that we are here on a woman's journey, they are not on our journey," says Tasha Simmons, a midwifery ward manager at the trust.  "They don't need to know that I've answered three emergency bells this morning, that's not important to them.  "What's important is I'm fully present with them to support them in their experience, with kindness and compassion."No-one starts a shift intending to provide care that is lacking in compassion.  The problem, say staff, is the pressure they are under - from the sheer number of people in Accident and Emergency to the complexity of many of the patients in hospital.  Remembering to treat each person with kindness in those circumstances can be a challenge, said Dr Adrian Marsh, an emergency medicine consultant at the Princess Royal Hospital.  There is a "high risk of emotional and compassion fatigue.  Day in, day out we have a significant amount of competing demands," he said.  "But there's been some research done that actually demonstrates if people are treated with compassion and empathy, they have less complications, [their] outcomes are better."Poppy's parents say that other NHS organisations and some universities have been in touch to explore whether they can incorporate Poppy's Promise into their teaching programme.  Their goal is to embed compassionate care throughout the health service.

schema.headline: Mum blamed for baby's death at Telford hospital calls for change in NHS
